Where it began

Kumar Sangakkara was born in Matale, in Sri Lanka's Central Province, on 27 October 1977, and grew up near Kandy, the youngest of four in a family that loved its sport, and all four children shone at Trinity College in Kandy.

Kumar had to choose. He sang in the choir and played the violin, and on the sports field it came down to tennis or cricket; the school's principal, asked for advice, said cricket. He became head boy, went on to read law at the University of Colombo, and joined Nondescripts. In 1999 he left his studies behind to tour South Africa with Sri Lanka A.

The player

He first played for Sri Lanka in July 2000, in a one-day match at Galle, and a fortnight later made his Test debut on the same ground against South Africa, keeping wicket as Sri Lanka won by an innings. Both his catches came off Muttiah Muralitharan, a combination that would become familiar.

In 134 Tests from 2000 to 2015 he made 12,400 runs at 57.41, with 38 hundreds and 52 fifties. In 2006 against South Africa he and Mahela Jayawardene added 624 for the third wicket, the biggest partnership in all first-class cricket, with his share 287. His best was 319 against Bangladesh in 2014, and he followed it with a hundred in the second innings. He captained Sri Lanka in 15 Tests and took them to the 2011 World Cup final, and three years later his unbeaten 52 won the final of the World Twenty20.

What made him special

He was a left-hander of real elegance, and he made double hundreds almost as a habit: by January 2015 he had 11 in Tests, one short of Don Bradman. In December 2007 he went to the top of the world Test batting rankings, and at the 2015 World Cup he became the first man to make four hundreds in a row at the tournament.

He did bowl the occasional off-break in Tests, though the wicket column stayed resolutely empty.

Away from the middle

Wisden chose him as the leading cricketer on the planet for 2011 and again for 2014, and in 2012 the ICC made him its Cricketer of the Year. He played for Surrey from 2015 to 2017, and in that last season he made five hundreds in a row. He went on to commentate for Sky Sports, served as President of MCC from 2019 to 2021, and coached Rajasthan Royals, taking them to the 2022 final of the Indian Premier League. In June 2021 he joined Muralitharan in the ICC Hall of Fame.

And finally

At the 2011 World Cup final the crowd was so loud that the match referee could not hear his call, and the toss had to be done again. For a man who chose cricket over the violin, being drowned out by an audience was perhaps a fair trade.
